newsitem.title: USA: Russia still wary on debt market opening - Livshits.
newsitem.headline: Russia still wary on debt market opening - Livshits.

text.p: Russia, under pressure to open further its government securities market to foreigners, is committed to liberalisation but questions remain over the timetable, Finance Minister Alexander Livshits said on Sunday.

Livshits, speaking as he arrived for a meeting of the International Monetary Fund's policy-making Interim Committee, said Russia remained concerned to avoid large-scale flows of funds which could disturb the market.
"The main thing for us is to avoid, even in the slightest respect, a situation analogous to Mexico," he told reporters.
The IMF, which earlier this year approved a $10 billion, three-year loan to Russia, wants Moscow to ease access to the market for non-residents.
It says the restrictions on access help keep interest rates high and crowd out badly needed investment.
"There is no problem about whether the market will be liberalised or not. The question is only in what form and at what pace this will happen," Livshits said.
He said the regime would be liberalised first for those investors who wished constantly to re-invest on the market.

Since August 15, Russia has allowed foreign investors to open special rouble accounts at designated banks to trade on the secondary market for GKO discount Treasury bills and to participate in primary auctions.
However, the rouble proceeds have to be reconverted at a rate related to a central bank forward rate. This limits the yield and allows the bank to control the outflow of money.

The government hopes the liberalisation will lead to a fall in yields. Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin has said he wants yields down to between 30 and 50 percent, depending on maturity, by the end of the year.

Livshits said he and Central Bank Chairman Sergei Dubinin had recently met foreign investors in Moscow over the issue and that the investors wanted a shorter period for the forward contract and no limitations on yields.
"There are other problems but it is simply a working situation,"he said.
Livshits acknowledged the funds attracted to the T-bill market were still relatively small.
"The stability of the market is the deciding issue,"he said.
